_Ulysses_ is divided into the three books (marked I, II, and III) and 18 episodes. The episodes do not have chapter headings or titles, and are numbered only in Gabler's edition. In the various editions, the breaks between episodes are indicated in different ways; in the Modern Library edition, for example, each episode begins at the top of a new page.

Joyce seems to have relished his book's obscurity, saying he had "put in so many enigmas and puzzles that it will keep the professors busy for centuries arguing over what I meant, and that's the only way of insuring [sic] one's immortality".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-18) The American judge who decided that _Ulysses_ was not obscene, [John M. Woolsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Woolsey "John M. Woolsey"), admitted that it "is not an easy book to read or to understand", and advised reading "a number of other books which have now become its satellites".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-19) One such book available at the time was Herbert Gorman's first book on Joyce, which included his own brief list of correspondences between _Ulysses_ and the _Odyssey_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-20) Another was [Stuart Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Gilbert "Stuart Gilbert")'s study of _Ulysses_, which included a [schema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_schema_for_Ulysses "Gilbert schema for Ulysses") of the novel Joyce created.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-21) Gilbert was later quoted in the legal brief prepared for the obscenity trial.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982666-22) Joyce had already sent [Carlo Linati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linati_schema_for_Ulysses "Linati schema for Ulysses") a different schema.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982521n-23) The Gilbert and Linati schemata made the links to the _Odyssey_ clearer and also explained the work's structure.

### Joyce and Homer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Joyce and Homer")]

The 18 episodes of _Ulysses_ "roughly correspond to the episodes in Homer's _[Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey "Odyssey")_".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-24) In Homer's epic, [Odysseus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus"), "a Greek hero of the [Trojan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War") ... took ten years to find his way from [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy") to his home on the island of [Ithaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ithaca_(island) "Ithaca (island)")".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-25) Homer's poem includes violent storms and a shipwreck, giants, monsters, gods, and goddesses, while Joyce's novel takes place during an ordinary day in early 20th-century Dublin. [Leopold Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Bloom "Leopold Bloom"), "a Jewish advertisement canvasser", corresponds to Odysseus in Homer's epic; [Stephen Dedalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Dedalus "Stephen Dedalus"), the protagonist of Joyce's earlier, largely autobiographical _[A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Portrait\_of\_the\_Artist\_as\_a\_Young\_Man "A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man")_, corresponds to Odysseus's son [Telemachus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"); and Bloom's wife [Molly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Bloom "Molly Bloom") corresponds to [Penelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope "Penelope"), Odysseus's wife, who waited 20 years for him to return.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-26)

_The Odyssey_ is divided into 24 books, which are divided into 3 parts of 4, 8, and 12 books. Although _Ulysses_ has fewer episodes, their division into 3 parts of 3, 12, and 3 episodes is determined by the tripartite division of _The Odyssey_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann19721%E2%80%932-27) Joyce referred to the episodes by their Homeric titles in his letters. The novel's text does not include the episode titles used below, which originate from the [Linati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linati_schema_for_Ulysses "Linati schema for Ulysses") and [Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_schema_for_Ulysses "Gilbert schema for Ulysses") schemata. Joyce scholars have drawn upon both to identify and explain the parallels between _Ulysses_ and _The Odyssey_.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1972-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKenner198719%E2%80%9330-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-31)

Scholars have argued that [Victor Bérard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_B%C3%A9rard "Victor Bérard")'s _Les Phéniciens et l'Odyssée_, which Joyce discovered in Zurich while writing _Ulysses_, influenced his creation of the novel's Homeric parallels.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-33) Bérard's theory that _The Odyssey_ had Semitic roots accords with Joyce's reincarnation of Odysseus as the Jewish Leopold Bloom.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982408-34)

[Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound") regarded the Homeric correspondences as "a scaffold, a means of construction, justified by the result, and justifiable by it only. The result is a triumph in form, in balance, a main schema with continuous weaving and arabesque."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-35) For [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot"), the Homeric correspondences had "the importance of a scientific discovery". He wrote, "In manipulating a continuous parallel between contemporaneity and antiquity... Mr. Joyce is pursuing a method which others must pursue after him." This method "is simply a way of controlling, of ordering, of giving a shape and significance to the immense panorama of futility and anarchy which is contemporary history".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-36)

[Edmund Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Wilson "Edmund Wilson") wrote, "The adventures of Ulysses ... do represent the ordinary man in nearly every common relation. Yet I cannot but feel that Mr. Joyce made a mistake to have the whole plan of his story depend on the structure of the _Odyssey_ rather than on the natural demands of the situation. ... His taste for symbolism is closely allied with his extraordinary poetic faculty for investing particular incidents with universal significance, nevertheless ... it sometimes overruns the bounds of art into an arid ingenuity which would make a mystic correspondence do duty for an artistic reason. The result is that one sometimes feels as if the brilliant succession of episodes were taking place on the periphery of a wheel which has no hub."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-A_review_of_James_Joyce's_Ulysses-37)

In the late 1930s Joyce told [Samuel Beckett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Beckett "Samuel Beckett"), "I may have over-systematized _Ulysses_."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982702-38) Around 1937, in a conversation with [Vladimir Nabokov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Nabokov "Vladimir Nabokov"), Joyce disparaged the use of mythology in modern literature. Nabokov replied, "But you employed Homer!" "A whim", Joyce said. When Nabokov pointed to his collaboration with Stuart Gilbert, Joyce replied, "A terrible mistake ... an advertisement for the book. I regret it very much."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982616-39)

The American literary scholar [William York Tindall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_York_Tindall "William York Tindall") has written, "Joyce considered Homer's myth the complete expression of man. ... Exile, home, humanity, and art, Joyce's concerns, found expression in Homer's _Odyssey_. ... But the Homeric pattern is only one level of the narrative Joyce composed. Another level is the Christian pattern. ... Bloom is not only Odysseus but Jesus-God. These traditional beliefs, however, are less important than the main level of Joyce's myth: the story of Stephen Dedalus and Mr. Bloom in Dublin or the present, the particular, and the personal. _Ulysses_ is a narrative composition of three levels, to which, by allusion, Joyce added others of less importance. His myth is not the _Odyssey_ but _Ulysses_."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-40)

### Joyce and Shakespeare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Joyce and Shakespeare")]

After Homer's _Odyssey_, the literary work _Ulysses_ parallels most closely is William Shakespeare's _[Hamlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlet "Hamlet")_. The play is mentioned in "[Telemachus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#Episode_1,_%22Telemachus%22)". _Hamlet_ is a symbol in the [Linati schema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linati_schema_for_Ulysses "Linati schema for Ulysses"). In [the Library episode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#Episode_9,_%22Scylla_and_Charybdis%22), [Stephen Dedalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Dedalus "Stephen Dedalus") puts forth a theory of _Hamlet_ based on 12 lectures, now lost, that Joyce gave in Trieste in 1912.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-41) Chief among the implied parallels with _Ulysses_ are Shakespeare and Joyce, [King Hamlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Hamlet "King Hamlet") and [Leopold Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Bloom "Leopold Bloom"), and [Prince Hamlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Hamlet "Prince Hamlet") and Stephen.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-42)

According to Stephen, Shakespeare has a double presence in _Hamlet_. The king is the mature Shakespeare; the prince is Shakespeare as a young man.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlamires196683%E2%80%9384-43) Stephen's insistence on Shakespeare's double presence in _Hamlet_ hints at Joyce's double presence in _Ulysses_.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlamires196683-44) Bloom is the mature Joyce; Stephen is Joyce as a young man.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELang199381-45) Other parallels with _Hamlet_ include Gertrude and Molly Bloom, Claudius and Buck Mulligan, and Claudius and Blazes Boylan.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETindall1959176-46)

Like Shakespeare, Dante was a major influence on Joyce.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-47) It has been argued that the interrelationship of Joyce, Dedalus, and Bloom is defined in the [Incarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incarnation_(Christianity) "Incarnation (Christianity)") doctrines Stephen lists in "Telemachus".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-48)

## Plot summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Plot summary")]

### Part I: Telemachia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Part I: Telemachia")]

#### Episode 1, "Telemachus"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Episode 1, \"Telemachus\"")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/James_Joyce_Tower_and_Museum3.JPG/250px-James_Joyce_Tower_and_Museum3.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Joyce_Tower_and_Museum3.JPG)

James Joyce's room in the [James Joyce Tower and Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Joyce_Tower_and_Museum "James Joyce Tower and Museum")

At 8 a.m., [Malachi "Buck" Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buck_Mulligan "Buck Mulligan"), a boisterous medical student, calls an aspiring writer, [Stephen Dedalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Dedalus "Stephen Dedalus"), up to the roof of the [Sandycove Martello tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Joyce_Tower_and_Museum "James Joyce Tower and Museum"), where they live. There is tension between Stephen and Mulligan: Stephen overheard Mulligan make a cruel remark about Stephen's recently deceased mother, and Mulligan has invited an English student, [Haines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haines_(character) "Haines (character)"), whom Stephen dislikes, to stay with them. The three men eat breakfast and walk to the shore, where Mulligan demands from Stephen the key to the tower and a loan. The three make plans to meet at a pub, The Ship, at 12:30pm. Departing, Stephen decides that he will not return to the tower that night, as Mulligan, the "usurper", has taken it over.

#### Episode 2, "Nestor"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Episode 2, \"Nestor\"")]

Stephen is teaching a history class on the victories of [Pyrrhus of Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrrhus_of_Epirus "Pyrrhus of Epirus"). After class, one student, [Cyril Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Sargent "Cyril Sargent"), stays behind so that Stephen can show him how to do a set of algebraic exercises. Stephen looks at Sargent's ugly face and tries to imagine Sargent's mother's love for him. He then visits [unionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unionism_in_Ireland "Unionism in Ireland") school headmaster [Garrett Deasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_Deasy "Garrett Deasy"), from whom he collects his pay. Deasy asks Stephen to take his long-winded letter about [foot-and-mouth disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot-and-mouth_disease "Foot-and-mouth disease") to a newspaper office for printing. The two discuss Irish history and Deasy lectures on what he believes is the role of Jews in the economy. As Stephen leaves, Deasy jokes that Ireland has "never persecuted the Jews" because the country "never let them in". This episode is the source of some of the novel's best-known lines, such as Dedalus's claim that "history is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake" and that God is "a shout in the street".

#### Episode 3, "Proteus"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Episode 3, \"Proteus\"")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/IMG_SandymountStrabd1461.jpg/250px-IMG_SandymountStrabd1461.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IMG_SandymountStrabd1461.jpg)

[Sandymount Strand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandymount_Strand "Sandymount Strand") looking across [Dublin Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Bay "Dublin Bay") to [Howth Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howth_Head "Howth Head")

Stephen walks along [Sandymount Strand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandymount_Strand "Sandymount Strand") for some time, mulling various philosophical concepts, his family, his life as a student in Paris, and his mother's death. As he reminisces he lies down among some rocks, watches a couple whose dog urinates behind a rock, scribbles some ideas for poetry and picks his nose. This chapter is characterised by a [stream of consciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_of_consciousness "Stream of consciousness") narrative style that changes focus wildly. Stephen's education is reflected in the many obscure references and foreign phrases employed in this episode, which have earned it a reputation for being one of the book's most difficult chapters.

### Part II: Odyssey

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Part II: Odyssey")]

#### Episode 4, "Calypso"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Episode 4, \"Calypso\"")]

The narrative shifts abruptly. The time is again 8 a.m., but the action has moved across the city and to the second protagonist of the book, Leopold Bloom, a part-Jewish advertising canvasser. The episode opens with the line "Mr. Leopold Bloom ate with relish the inner organs of beasts and fowls." After starting to prepare breakfast, Bloom decides to walk to a butcher to buy a mutton kidney. Returning home, he prepares breakfast and brings it with the mail to his wife [Molly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Bloom "Molly Bloom") as she lounges in bed. One of the letters is from her concert manager [Blazes Boylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blazes_Boylan "Blazes Boylan"), with whom she is planning to begin an affair. Bloom reads a letter from their daughter [Milly Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milly_Bloom "Milly Bloom"), who tells him about her progress in the photography business in Mullingar. The episode closes with Bloom reading a magazine story titled "Matcham's Masterstroke", by Mr. Philip Beaufoy, while defecating in the outhouse.

#### Episode 5, "Lotus Eaters"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Episode 5, \"Lotus Eaters\"")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Ulysses_undertaker.jpg/250px-Ulysses_undertaker.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ulysses_undertaker.jpg)

Several Dublin businesses note that they were mentioned in _Ulysses_, like this [undertakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_director "Funeral director").

While making his way to [Westland Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westland_Row "Westland Row") post office Bloom is tormented by the knowledge that Molly will welcome Boylan into their bed later that day. At the post office he surreptitiously collects a love letter from one 'Martha Clifford' addressed to his pseudonym, 'Henry Flower'. He meets an acquaintance, and while they chat, Bloom attempts to ogle a woman wearing stockings, but is prevented by a passing tram. Next, he reads the letter from Martha Clifford and tears up the envelope in an alley. He wanders into a Catholic church during a service and muses on theology. The priest has the letters [I.N.R.I.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus,_King_of_the_Jews "Jesus, King of the Jews") or [I.H.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit_emblem "Jesuit emblem") on his back; Molly had told Bloom that they meant _I have sinned_ or _I have suffered_, and _Iron nails ran in_. He buys a bar of lemon soap from a chemist (Sweny's Pharmacy). He then meets another acquaintance, [Bantam Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantam_Lyons "Bantam Lyons"), who mistakenly takes him to be offering a racing tip for the horse _Throwaway_. Finally, Bloom heads towards the [baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_Turkish_bath "Victorian Turkish bath").

#### Episode 6, "Hades"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Episode 6, \"Hades\"")]

The episode begins with Bloom entering a funeral carriage with three others, including Stephen's father. They drive to [Paddy Dignam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Dignam "Paddy Dignam")'s funeral, making small talk on the way. The carriage passes both Stephen and Blazes Boylan. There is discussion of various forms of death and burial. Bloom is preoccupied by thoughts of his dead infant son, Rudy, and the suicide of his own father. They enter the chapel for the service and subsequently leave with the coffin cart. Bloom sees a mysterious man wearing a [Mackintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackintosh_(raincoat) "Mackintosh (raincoat)") raincoat during the burial. Bloom continues to reflect upon death, but at the end of the episode rejects morbid thoughts to embrace "warm fullblooded life".

#### Episode 7, "Aeolus"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Episode 7, \"Aeolus\"")]

At the office of the _[Freeman's Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeman's\_Journal "Freeman's Journal")_, Bloom attempts to place an ad. Although initially encouraged by the editor, he is unsuccessful. Stephen arrives bringing Deasy's letter about foot-and-mouth disease, but Stephen and Bloom do not meet. Stephen leads the editor and others to a pub, relating an anecdote on the way about "two Dublin vestals". The episode is broken into short segments by newspaper-style headlines, and is characterised by an abundance of rhetorical figures and devices.

#### Episode 8, "Lestrygonians"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Episode 8, \"Lestrygonians\"")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Fietsen_staan_tegen_de_stoeprand_geparkeerd_in_een_straat_in_Dublin%2C_Bestanddeelnr_191-0870.jpg/250px-Fietsen_staan_tegen_de_stoeprand_geparkeerd_in_een_straat_in_Dublin%2C_Bestanddeelnr_191-0870.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fietsen_staan_tegen_de_stoeprand_geparkeerd_in_een_straat_in_Dublin,_Bestanddeelnr_191-0870.jpg)

Davy Byrne's Pub, Dublin, where Bloom consumes a gorgonzola cheese sandwich and a glass of burgundy

Bloom's thoughts are peppered with references to food as lunchtime approaches. He meets an old flame, hears news of Mina Purefoy's labour, and helps a blind boy cross the street. He enters the restaurant of the Burton Hotel, where he is revolted by the sight of men eating like animals. He goes instead to [Davy Byrne's pub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_Byrne's_pub "Davy Byrne's pub"), where he consumes a gorgonzola cheese sandwich and a glass of burgundy, and muses upon the early days of his relationship with Molly and how the marriage has declined: "Me. And me now." Bloom's thoughts touch on what goddesses and gods eat and drink. He ponders whether the statues of Greek goddesses in the [National Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Ireland "National Museum of Ireland") have anuses as do mortals. On leaving the pub Bloom heads toward the museum, but spots Boylan across the street and, panicking, rushes into the gallery across the street from the museum.

#### Episode 9, "Scylla and Charybdis"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Episode 9, \"Scylla and Charybdis\"")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Dublin%2C_Nationalbiblioteket%2C_Nordisk_familjebok.png/250px-Dublin%2C_Nationalbiblioteket%2C_Nordisk_familjebok.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dublin,_Nationalbiblioteket,_Nordisk_familjebok.png)

[National Library of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_of_Ireland "National Library of Ireland")

At the [National Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_of_Ireland "National Library of Ireland"), Stephen explains to some scholars his biographical theory of the works of Shakespeare, especially _[Hamlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlet "Hamlet")_, which he argues are based largely on the posited adultery of [Shakespeare's wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hathaway_(wife_of_Shakespeare) "Anne Hathaway (wife of Shakespeare)"). Buck Mulligan arrives and interrupts to read out the telegram that Stephen had sent him indicating that he would not make their planned rendezvous at The Ship. Bloom enters the National Library to look up an old copy of the ad he has been trying to place. He passes in between Stephen and Mulligan as they exit the library at the end of the episode.

#### Episode 10, "Wandering Rocks"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Episode 10, \"Wandering Rocks\"")]

In this episode, nineteen short [vignettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vignette_(literature) "Vignette (literature)") depict the movements of various characters, major and minor, through the streets of Dublin. The episode begins by following [Father Conmee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Conmee "John Conmee"), a Jesuit priest, on his trip north, and ends with an account of the cavalcade of the [Lord Lieutenant of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Lieutenant_of_Ireland "Lord Lieutenant of Ireland"), [William Ward, Earl of Dudley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ward,_Earl_of_Dudley "William Ward, Earl of Dudley"), through the streets, which is encountered by several characters from the novel.

#### Episode 11, "Sirens"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Episode 11, \"Sirens\"")]

In this episode, dominated by motifs of music, Bloom has dinner with Stephen's uncle at the Ormond hotel, while Molly's lover, Blazes Boylan, proceeds to his rendezvous with her. While dining, Bloom listens to the singing of Stephen's father and others, watches the seductive barmaids, and composes a reply to Martha Clifford's letter.

#### Episode 12, "Cyclops"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Episode 12, \"Cyclops\"")]

This episode is narrated by an unnamed inhabitant of Dublin who works as a debt collector. The narrator goes to [Barney Kiernan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ulysses_characters#Kiernan "List of Ulysses characters")'s pub where he meets a character referred to only as "[The Citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Citizen_(character) "The Citizen (character)")". This character is believed to be a satirisation of [Michael Cusack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cusack_(Gaelic_Athletic_Association) "Michael Cusack (Gaelic Athletic Association)"), a founder member of the [Gaelic Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_Athletic_Association "Gaelic Athletic Association").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-irishtimes-1.1145091-49) When Leopold Bloom enters the pub, he is berated by the Citizen, a fierce [Fenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenian "Fenian") and antisemite. The episode ends with Bloom reminding the Citizen that his Saviour was a Jew. As Bloom leaves the pub, the Citizen throws a biscuit tin at Bloom's head, but misses. The episode is marked by extended tangents made in voices other than that of the unnamed narrator; these include streams of legal jargon, a report of a boxing match, Biblical passages, and elements of Irish mythology.

#### Episode 13, "Nausicaa"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Episode 13, \"Nausicaa\"")]

All the action of the episode takes place on the rocks of Sandymount Strand, the shoreline that Stephen visited in Episode 3. A young woman, Gerty MacDowell, is seated on the rocks with her two friends, Cissy Caffrey and Edy Boardman. The girls are taking care of three children, a baby, and four-year-old twins named Tommy and Jacky. Gerty contemplates love, marriage and femininity as night falls. The reader is gradually made aware that Bloom is watching her from a distance. Gerty teases the onlooker by exposing her legs and underwear, and Bloom, in turn, masturbates. Bloom's masturbatory climax is echoed by the fireworks at the nearby bazaar. As Gerty leaves, Bloom realises that she has a lame leg, and believes this is the reason she has been "left on the shelf". After several mental digressions he decides to visit Mina Purefoy at the maternity hospital. It is uncertain how much of the episode is Gerty's thoughts, and how much is Bloom's sexual fantasy. Some believe that the episode is divided into two halves: the first half the highly romanticized viewpoint of Gerty, and the other half that of the older and more realistic Bloom.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-:0-50) Joyce himself said, however, that "nothing happened between [Gerty and Bloom]. It all took place in Bloom's imagination".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-:0-50)_Nausicaa_ attracted immense notoriety while the book was being published in serial form. It has also attracted great attention from scholars of disability in literature.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-51) The style of the first half of the episode borrows from (and parodies) romance magazines and novelettes. Bloom's contemplation of Gerty parodies Dedalus's vision of the wading girl at the seashore in _A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man_.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982359n-53)

#### Episode 14, "Oxen of the Sun"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Episode 14, \"Oxen of the Sun\"")]

Bloom visits the maternity hospital where Mina Purefoy is giving birth, and finally meets Stephen, who has been drinking with his medical student friends and is awaiting the promised arrival of Buck Mulligan. As the only father in the group of men, Bloom is concerned about Mina Purefoy in her labour. He starts thinking about his wife and the births of his two children. He also thinks about the loss of his only 'heir', Rudy. The young men become boisterous, and start discussing such topics as fertility, contraception and abortion. There is also a suggestion that Milly, Bloom's daughter, is in a relationship with one of the young men, Bannon. They continue on to a pub to continue drinking, following the successful birth of a son to Mina Purefoy. This chapter is remarkable for Joyce's wordplay, which, among other things, recapitulates the entire history of the English language. After a short incantation, the episode starts with latinate prose, [Anglo-Saxon alliteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_poetry "Old English poetry"), and moves on through parodies of, among others, [Malory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Malory "Thomas Malory"), the [King James Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Bible "King James Bible"), [Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan"), [Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys"), [Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe"), [Sterne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Sterne "Laurence Sterne"), [Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Walpole "Horace Walpole"), [Gibbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Gibbon "Edward Gibbon"), [Dickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens "Charles Dickens"), and [Carlyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carlyle "Thomas Carlyle"), before concluding in a Joycean version of contemporary slang. The development of the English language in the episode is believed to be aligned with the nine-month gestation period of the foetus in the womb.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-54)

#### Episode 15, "Circe"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Episode 15, \"Circe\"")]

Episode 15 is written as a play script, complete with stage directions. The plot is frequently interrupted by "hallucinations" experienced by Stephen and Bloom—fantastic manifestations of the fears and passions of the two characters. Stephen and his friend Lynch walk into [Nighttown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monto "Monto"), Dublin's [red-light district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red-light_district "Red-light district"). Bloom pursues them and eventually finds them at [Bella Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bella_Cohen "Bella Cohen")'s brothel where, in the company of her workers including [Zoe Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoe_Higgins "Zoe Higgins"), [Florry Talbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florry_Talbot "Florry Talbot") and [Kitty Ricketts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitty_Ricketts "Kitty Ricketts"), he has a series of hallucinations regarding his [sexual fetishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_fetishes "Sexual fetishes"), fantasies and transgressions. In one of these hallucinations, Bloom is put in the dock to answer charges by a variety of sadistic, accusing women including [Mrs Yelverton Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs_Yelverton_Barry "Mrs Yelverton Barry"), [Mrs Bellingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs_Bellingham "Mrs Bellingham") and the Hon [Mrs Mervyn Talboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs_Mervyn_Talboys "Mrs Mervyn Talboys"). In another of Bloom's hallucinations, he is crowned king of his own city, which is called Bloomusalem—Bloom imagines himself being loved and admired by Bloomusalem's citizens, but then imagines himself being accused of various charges. As a result, he is burnt at the stake and several citizens pay their respects to him as he dies.

Then the hallucination ends, Bloom finds himself next to Zoe, and the two talk. After they talk, Bloom continues to encounter other miscellaneous hallucinations, including one in which he converses with his grandfather Lipoti Virag, who lectures him about sex, among other things. At the end of the hallucination, Bloom is speaking with some prostitutes when he hears a sound coming from downstairs. He hears heels clacking on the staircase, and he observes what appears to be a male form passing down the staircase. He speaks with Zoe and Kitty for a moment, and then sees Bella Cohen come into the brothel. He observes her appearance and talks with her for a little while. But this conversation subsequently begins another hallucination, in which Bloom imagines Bella to be a man named Mr. Bello and Bloom imagines himself to be a woman. In this fantasy, Bloom imagines himself (or "herself", in the hallucination) being dominated by Bello, who both sexually and verbally humiliates Bloom. Bloom also interacts with other imaginary characters in this scene before the hallucination ends.

After the hallucination ends, Bloom sees Stephen overpay at the brothel, and decides to hold onto the rest of Stephen's money for safekeeping. Stephen hallucinates that his mother's rotting cadaver has risen up from the floor to confront him. He cries _[Non serviam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non\_serviam "Non serviam")!_, uses his walking stick to smash a chandelier, and flees the room. Bloom quickly pays Bella for the damage, then runs after Stephen. He finds Stephen engaged in an argument with an English soldier, [Private Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Wilfrid_Carr "Henry Wilfrid Carr"), who, after hearing Stephen utter a perceived insult to King [Edward VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VII "Edward VII"), punches him. The police arrive and the crowd disperses. As Bloom tends to Stephen, he has a hallucination of his deceased son, Rudy, as an 11-year-old.

### Part III: Nostos

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Part III: Nostos")]

#### Episode 16, "Eumaeus"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Episode 16, \"Eumaeus\"")]

Bloom takes Stephen to a cabman's shelter near [Butt Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butt_Bridge "Butt Bridge") to restore him to his senses. There, they encounter a drunken sailor, D. B. Murphy (W. B. Murphy in the 1922 text). The episode is dominated by the motif of confusion and mistaken identity, with Bloom, Stephen and Murphy's identities being repeatedly called into question. The narrative's rambling and laboured style in this episode reflects the protagonists' nervous exhaustion and confusion.

#### Episode 17, "Ithaca"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Episode 17, \"Ithaca\"")]

Bloom returns home with Stephen, makes him a cup of [cocoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_chocolate "Hot chocolate"), discusses cultural and linguistic differences between them, considers the possibility of publishing Stephen's parable stories, and offers him a place to stay for the night. Stephen refuses Bloom's offer and is ambiguous in response to Bloom's proposal of future meetings. The two men urinate in the backyard, Stephen departs and wanders off into the night,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-55) and Bloom goes to bed, where Molly is sleeping. She wakes and asks him about his day. The episode is written in the form of a rigidly organised and "mathematical" [catechism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechism "Catechism") of 309 questions and answers, and was reportedly Joyce's favourite episode in the novel. The deep descriptions range from questions of astronomy to the trajectory of urination and include a list of 25 men that purports to be the "preceding series" of Molly's suitors and Bloom's reflections on them. While describing events apparently chosen randomly in ostensibly precise mathematical or scientific terms, the episode is rife with errors, many or most of them intentional on Joyce's part.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-mac-56)

#### Episode 18, "Penelope"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Episode 18, \"Penelope\"")]

The final episode consists of Molly Bloom's thoughts as she lies in bed next to her husband. The episode uses a stream-of-consciousness technique in eight paragraphs and lacks punctuation. Molly thinks about Boylan and Bloom, her past admirers, including Lieutenant [Stanley G. Gardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_G._Gardner "Stanley G. Gardner"), the events of the day, her childhood in Gibraltar, and her curtailed singing career. She also hints at a lesbian relationship in her youth with a childhood friend, Hester Stanhope. These thoughts are occasionally interrupted by distractions, such as a train whistle or the need to urinate. Molly is surprised by the early arrival of her menstrual period, which she ascribes to her vigorous sex with Boylan. The episode concludes with Molly's remembrance of Bloom's marriage proposal, and of her acceptance: "he asked me would I yes to say yes my mountain flower and first I put my arms around him yes and drew him down to me so he could feel my breasts all perfume yes and his heart was going like mad and yes I said yes I will Yes."

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Censorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Censorship")]

Main articles: [Obscenity trial of Ulysses in _The Little Review_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obscenity_trial_of_Ulysses_in_The_Little_Review "Obscenity trial of Ulysses in The Little Review") and [_United States v. One Book Called Ulysses_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._One_Book_Called_Ulysses "United States v. One Book Called Ulysses")

Written over a seven-year period from 1914 to 1921, _Ulysses_ was [serialised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_(literature) "Serial (literature)") in the American journal _[The Little Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Little\_Review "The Little Review")_ from 1918 to 1920,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-57) when the publication of [the "Nausicaa" episode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#Episode_13,_%22Nausicaa%22) led to [a prosecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obscenity_trial_of_Ulysses_in_The_Little_Review "Obscenity trial of Ulysses in The Little Review") for obscenity under the [Comstock Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comstock_Act "Comstock Act") of 1873, which made it illegal to circulate materials deemed obscene in the U.S. mail.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982502%E2%80%93504-58) In 1919, sections of the novel also appeared in the London literary journal _[The Egoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Egoist\_(periodical) "The Egoist (periodical)")_, but the novel itself was banned in the United Kingdom until 1936.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-59) Joyce had resolved that the book would be published on his 40th birthday, 2 February 1922, and Sylvia Beach, Joyce's publisher in Paris, received the first three copies from the printer that morning.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllmann1982523%E2%80%93524-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-JJC-61)

The 1920 prosecution in the US was brought after _The Little Review_ serialised a passage of the book depicting characters masturbating. Three earlier chapters had been banned by the US Post Office, but it was Secretary of the [New York Society for the Suppression of Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Society_for_the_Suppression_of_Vice "New York Society for the Suppression of Vice")[John S. Sumner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_S._Sumner "John S. Sumner") who instigated this legal action.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-62) The Post Office did partially suppress the "Nausicaa" edition of _The Little Review_.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-63) Legal historian [Edward de Grazia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_de_Grazia "Edward de Grazia") has argued that few readers would have been fully aware of the masturbation in the text, given the metaphoric language.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-64) Irene Gammel extends this argument to suggest that the obscenity allegations against _The Little Review_ were influenced by the [Baroness Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroness_Elsa "Baroness Elsa")'s more explicit poetry, which had appeared alongside the serialisation of _Ulysses_.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-65) At the [trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obscenity_trial_of_Ulysses_in_The_Little_Review "Obscenity trial of Ulysses in The Little Review"), in 1921, the magazine was declared obscene, and as a result _Ulysses_ was effectively banned in the United States. Throughout the 1920s, the [United States Post Office Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") burned copies of the novel.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-66)

In 1932, Random House and lawyer [Morris Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Ernst "Morris Ernst") arranged to import the French edition and have a copy seized by Customs. Random House contested the seizure, and in _[United States v. One Book Called Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United\_States\_v.\_One\_Book\_Called\_Ulysses "United States v. One Book Called Ulysses")_, U.S. District Judge [John M. Woolsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Woolsey "John M. Woolsey") ruled that the book was not pornographic and therefore could not be obscene,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-67) a decision Stuart Gilbert called "epoch-making".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-68) The [Second Circuit Court of Appeals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Circuit_Court_of_Appeals "Second Circuit Court of Appeals") affirmed the ruling in 1934.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-69) The U.S. thus became the first English-speaking country where the book was freely available. Although [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland")'s [Censorship of Publications Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_of_Publications_Board_(Ireland) "Censorship of Publications Board (Ireland)") never banned _Ulysses_, a customs loophole prevented it from being allowed into Ireland.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-JJC-61)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-71) It was first openly available in Ireland in the 1960s.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-72)

### Critical reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Critical reception")]

In 1922, [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound") wrote, "All men should 'Unite to give praise to _Ulysses_'; those who will not, may content themselves with a place in the lower intellectual orders." He claimed that in writing _Ulysses_, "this super-novel", Joyce surpassed [Gustave Flaubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Flaubert "Gustave Flaubert"), [Miguel de Cervantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes "Miguel de Cervantes"), [Henry James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James "Henry James"), and [Marcel Proust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Proust "Marcel Proust"), concluding that, besides [François Rabelais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Rabelais "François Rabelais"), he "can think of no other prose writer whose proportional status in pan-literature is not modified by the advent of _Ulysses_".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-73)

In a 1922 review in _[The Outlook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outlook\_(British\_magazine) "The Outlook (British magazine)")_, the British novelist [Arnold Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Bennett "Arnold Bennett") expressed his lack of admiration for Joyce detailing one day in 700 pages. He wrote, "Given sufficient time, paper, childish caprice, and obstinacy, one might easily write over seven thousand pages about twenty hours of life." Bennett also opposed [Valery Larbaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valery_Larbaud "Valery Larbaud")'s view that Joyce elaborately planned and organized the day he wrote about. He wrote that Joyce "apparently thinks there is something truly artistic and high minded in playing the lout to the innocent and defenseless reader. As a fact, there isn't ... After all, to comprehend _Ulysses_ is not among the recognized learned professions, and nobody should give his entire existence to the job." Bennett acknowledged that Joyce's "verbal method can be justified" since he is "trying to reproduce the thoughts of personage", but called the details "trivial and perfectly futile in the narrative".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-:1-74)

In April 1922, writing in _[The Nation and Athenaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nation\_and\_Athenaeum "The Nation and Athenaeum")_, English writer [John Middleton Murry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Middleton_Murry "John Middleton Murry") called Joyce "a genius of the very highest order, strictly comparable to Goethe or Dostoevsky…_Ulysses_ is, fundamentally (though it is much else besides), an immense, a prodigious self-laceration, the tearing away from himself, by a half-demented man of genius, of inhibitions and limitations which have grown to be flesh of his flesh…Mr. Joyce has made the superhuman effort to empty the whole of his consciousness into it…[But he has become] the victim of his own anarchy….[Joyce] is the man with the bomb who would blow what remains of Europe into the sky…This transcendental buffoonery, this sudden uprush of the _vis comica_ into a world where in the tragic incompatibility of the practical and the instinctive is embodied, is a very great achievement."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-75)

The next month, in the _[Sunday Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Express "Sunday Express")_, newspaper editor [James Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Douglas_(journalist) "James Douglas (journalist)") called _Ulysses_ "the most infamously obscene book in ancient or modern literature. ... All the secret sewers of vice are canalized in its flood of unimaginable thoughts, images and pornographic words. And its unclean lunacies are larded with appalling and revolting blasphemies directed against the Christian religion and against the name of Christ—blasphemies hitherto associated with the most degraded orgies of Satanism and the Black Mass."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-76)

In a 1922 review in _[The New Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Republic "The New Republic")_, literary critic [Edmund Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Wilson "Edmund Wilson") wrote, "_Ulysses_ is a work of high genius. Its importance seems to me to lie ... in its once more setting the standard of the novel so high that it need not be ashamed to take its place beside poetry and drama. _Ulysses_ has the effect at once of making everything else look brassy. Since I have read it, the texture of other novelists seems intolerably loose and careless; when I come suddenly unawares upon a page that I have written myself I quake like a guilty thing surprised. ... Who else has had the supreme devotion and accomplished the definitive beauty? If he has really laid down his pen never to take it up again he must know that the hand which laid it down upon the great affirmative of Mrs. Bloom, though it never write another word, is already the hand of a master."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-A_review_of_James_Joyce's_Ulysses-37)

In a 1922 review in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, [Joseph Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Collins_(neurologist) "Joseph Collins (neurologist)") wrote, "_Ulysses_ is the most important contribution that has been made to fictional literature in the twentieth century. ... It is likely that there is no one writing English today that could parallel Mr. Joyce's feat, and it is also likely that few would care to do it were they capable. ... When a master technician of words and phrases sets himself the task of revealing the product of the unconscious mind of a moral monster, a pervert and an invert, an apostate to his race and his religion, the simulacrum of a man who has neither cultural background nor personal self-respect, who can neither be taught by experience nor lessoned by example, as Mr. Joyce has done in drawing the picture of Leopold Bloom, and giving a faithful reproduction of his thoughts, purposeful, vagrant and obsessive, he undoubtedly knew full well what he was undertaking, and how unacceptable the vile contents of that unconscious mind would be to ninety-nine men out of a hundred, and how incensed they would be at having the disgusting product thrown in their faces. But that has nothing to do with that with which I am here concerned, viz., has the job been done well and is it a work of art, to which there can be only an affirmative answer."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-77)

In 1922, the writer and Irish nationalist [Shane Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Leslie "Shane Leslie") called _Ulysses_ "literary Bolshevism ... experimental, anti-conventional, anti-Christian, chaotic, totally unmoral".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-78) In the same year, [Sisley Huddleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisley_Huddleston "Sisley Huddleston") wrote in _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_: "I confess that I cannot see how the work upon which Mr Joyce spent seven strenuous years, years of wrestling and of agony, can ever be given to the public. ... This is undoubtedly an obscene book; but that, says Mr Joyce, is not his fault. If the thoughts of men and women are such as may be properly described as obscene then how can you show what life is unless you put in the obscenity." Molly Bloom's monologue, Leslie wrote, is "the vilest [chapter] according to ordinary standards, in all literature. And yet its very obscenity is somehow beautiful and wrings the soul to pity. Is that not high art? I cannot, however, believe that sex plays such a preponderant part in life as Mr Joyce represents. He may aim at putting everything in, but he has, of course, like everybody else, selected carefully what he puts in. Has he not exaggerated the vulgarity and magnified the madness of mankind and the mysterious materiality of the universe?"[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-79)

In a 1923 review, [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf "Virginia Woolf") wrote, "_Ulysses_ was a memorable catastrophe—immense in daring, terrific in disaster."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-80) In _[The Dial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dial "The Dial")_ the same year, [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") wrote: "I hold [_Ulysses_] to be the most important expression which the present age has found; it is a book to which we are all indebted, and from which none of us can escape." He added that Joyce was not at fault if people after him did not understand it: "The next generation is responsible for its own soul; a man of genius is responsible to his peers, not to a studio full of uneducated and undisciplined coxcombs."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-81)

In his 1930 book-length study of the novel, [Stuart Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Gilbert "Stuart Gilbert") said that the "personages of _Ulysses_ are _not_ fictitious" but that "these people are as they must be; they act, we see, according to some _lex eterna_, an ineluctable condition of their very existence". Through these characters Joyce "achieves a coherent and integral interpretation of life".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-82)

In _[Axel's Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel's\_Castle "Axel's Castle")_ (1931), [Edmund Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Wilson "Edmund Wilson") noted that _Ulysses_ attempts to render "as precisely and as directly as it is possible in words to do, what our participation in life is like—or rather, what it seems to us like as from moment to moment we live".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-83)

Addressing the first All-Union Congress of Soviet Writers in 1934, the writer and communist revolutionary [Karl Radek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Radek "Karl Radek") called _Ulysses_ "a heap of dung, crawling with worms, photographed by a cinema camera through a microscope".[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-84) Writing in _[America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America\_(magazine) "America (magazine)")_ magazine that year, [Francis X. Talbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_X._Talbot "Francis X. Talbot") vehemently decried Judge Woolsey's recent decision that _Ulysses_ was not obscene, adding, "Only a person who had been a Catholic, only one with an incurably diseased mind, could be so diabolically venomous toward God, toward the Blessed Sacrament, toward the Virgin Mary."[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-americamagazine.org-85)

In _Irish Literary Portraits_ (1935), [John Eglinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Eglinton "John Eglinton") characterized _Ulysses_ as an act of revenge: "I am convinced that the only person concerned in the narrative who comes out as a real hero is the author himself. What kind of hero after all is brought to mind by the name Ulysses if not a hero long absent from his kingdom, returning, after being the sport of the gods for ten years, in triumph and vengeance? And it was after nearly as many years of absence as Ulysses from the country 'which belonged to him' that Joyce turned up again for us in Dublin, with a vengeance! ... Endued ... with the elemental diabolism of Ulysses, he was transfigured. A thousand unexpected faculties and gay devices were liberated in his soul. The discovery of a new method in literary art, in which the pen is no longer the slave of logic and rhetoric, made of this Berlitz School teacher a kind of public danger, threatening to the corporate existence of 'literature' as established in the minds and affections of the older generation. ... Our Romano-Celtic Joyce nurses an ironic detachment from the whole of the English tradition. Indeed, he is its enemy. ... It must have seemed to him that he held English, his country's spiritual enemy, in the hollow of his hand, for the English language too came at his call to do his bidding. ... This language found itself constrained by its new master to perform tasks to which it was unaccustomed in the service of pure literature; against the grain it was forced to reproduce Joyce's fantasies in all kinds of juxtapositions, neologisms, amalgamations, truncations, words that are only found scrawled up in public lavatories, obsolete words, words in limbo or belike in the womb of time."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-86)

In a 1946 essay, Irene Hendry identified four distinct [epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_(literature) "Epiphany (literature)") techniques in Joyce's work, noting their use in _Ulysses_, from the simplest device, such as the revelation of Gerty Macdowell's limp, to the more complex, such as the bowl symbolism in "Telemachus". Cited as an example of Joyce's major epiphany technique—_[quidditas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quidditas "Quidditas")_ produced directly—is the revelation of Molly Bloom as "female essence".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-87)

In his first book on Joyce, the American scholar [William York Tindall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_York_Tindall "William York Tindall") wrote, "Since the naturalists tried to establish reality, they were descriptive. Before perfecting his art, Joyce tried this method. The Dublin of _[Dubliners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubliners "Dubliners")_ and its people are described. But almost abandoning description in _Ulysses_ Joyce evoked place and people. He established his characters by what they say; and his places, named but not described, live in the minds of his characters. Yet no place is more solid than Joyce's Dublin and no characters are more substantial. During his walk along the beach, Stephen exercises his descriptive powers on what he sees and hears. Gerty MacDowell's scene, which concerns the eye, is suitably pictorial. The catalogue of externals in Mr. Bloom's parlor is not naturalistic but a parody of naturalism and its reduction to absurdity. ... Joyce did not approach things directly like a naturalist but indirectly, through correspondence or analogy, as a symbolist."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-88)

In his second book on Joyce, Tindall wrote, "It is certain that, careful of external details, Joyce observed his city as a naturalist would. ... Yet, in _Ulysses_, as in the earlier works, he used these particulars to suggest inner or general things—in the manner of Baudelaire and Flaubert. Such usage is symbolist; for a symbol is a common thing, closely observed, suggesting other things. An observer of things, Joyce saw something else within them and beyond, something they embodied and showed forth. That much is plain, let critics quarrel as they will. And it is plain that, however reliant upon details of Dublin, Joyce called again upon parallel and motif to enlarge his particulars and hold them together. ... The riddling motifs of _Ulysses_ are complicated in turn by allusion, quotation, and single images or charged words—like those in _A Portrait_ or, better, since _Ulysses_ is a kind of poem, like those in 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETindall1959127,_131-89)

In his book-length study of _Ulysses_ (1961), the Australian scholar S. L. Goldberg argued that interior monologue in _Ulysses_ was rooted in Joyce's epiphany technique. For Goldberg, the epiphany is "the real artistic (and dramatic) unit of Joyce's 'stream-of-consciousness' writing. What he renders dramatically are minds engaged in the apprehension of epiphanies—the elements of meaning apprehended in life."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-90)

In a 1965 interview, novelist [Vladimir Nabokov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Nabokov "Vladimir Nabokov") called _Ulysses_ "a divine work of art [that] will live on despite the academic nonentities who turn it into a collection of symbols or Greek myths." He named it the greatest masterpiece of 20th-century prose.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-91) In a 1966 interview, he said, "it towers above the rest of Joyce's writing" with "noble originality and unique lucidity of thought and style".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-92)

Psychology professor Charles Fernyhough called _Ulysses_ "the archetypal stream of consciousness novel".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-93)

Joyce uses "metaphors, symbols, ambiguities, and overtones which gradually link themselves together so as to form a network of connections binding the whole" work.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-Blamires-94) This system of connections gives the novel a wide, more universal significance, as "Leopold Bloom becomes a modern Ulysses, an Everyman in a Dublin which becomes a microcosm of the world."[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-95)

The American author [Michael Chabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Chabon "Michael Chabon") wrote, "_Ulysses_ struck me, most of all, as a book of life; every sentence, even those that laid bare the doubt, despair, shame, or vanity of its characters, seemed to have been calibrated to assert, in keeping with the project of the work as a whole, the singularity and worth of even the most humdrum and throwaway of human days."[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-96)

_[Time Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-97)[Modern Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Library "Modern Library"),[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-98)_[Folha de S.Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folha\_de\_S.Paulo "Folha de S.Paulo")_[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-99) and _[CounterPunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CounterPunch "CounterPunch")_[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-100) have all published lists ranking _Ulysses_ as the greatest novel of the 20th century.

## Publication history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Publication history")]

See also: [Translations of Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translations_of_Ulysses "Translations of Ulysses")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Plaque%2C_12_Rue_Od%C3%A9on%2C_Paris_May_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Plaque%2C_12_Rue_Od%C3%A9on%2C_Paris_May_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plaque,_12_Rue_Od%C3%A9on,_Paris_May_2014_(cropped).jpg)

Memorial plaque, at 12 [Rue de l'Odéon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rue_de_l'Od%C3%A9on "Rue de l'Odéon"), [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_arrondissement_of_Paris "6th arrondissement of Paris") (the original location of [Shakespeare and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare_and_Company_(1919%E2%80%931941) "Shakespeare and Company (1919–1941)")): "In 1922, in this house, [Sylvia Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Beach "Sylvia Beach") published _Ulysses_ by James Joyce. J.J.S.S.F." (James Joyce Society of Sweden and Finland)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-jstor/26283610-101)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/James_Joyce_Ulysses_1st_Edition_1922_GB.jpg/250px-James_Joyce_Ulysses_1st_Edition_1922_GB.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Joyce_Ulysses_1st_Edition_1922_GB.jpg)

_Ulysses_ by James Joyce, Paris: Shakespeare, 1922

The publication history of _Ulysses_ is complex. There have been at least 18 editions, and variations among different impressions of each edition.

According to Joyce scholar Jack Dalton, the first edition of _Ulysses_ contained over 2,000 errors.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-102) As subsequent editions attempted to correct these mistakes, they would often add more, due in part to the difficulty of separating non-authorial errors from Joyce's deliberate "errors" devised to challenge the reader.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-mac-56)

Notable editions include:[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-103)

*   Paris: Shakespeare and Company, 1922: The private,[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-bbc/m001bvp2-104) first edition published in Paris on 2 February 1922 (Joyce's 40th birthday) by Sylvia Beach's [Shakespeare and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare_and_Company_(1919%E2%80%931941) "Shakespeare and Company (1919–1941)"). Beach commissioned [Maurice Darantiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Darantiere?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maurice Darantiere (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice%20Darantiere "fr:Maurice Darantiere")] in [Dijon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijon "Dijon") to print 1,000 numbered copies consisting of 100 signed copies on Dutch handmade paper (350 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc#French_franc "Franc")), 150 numbered copies on [vergé d'Arches paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arches_paper "Arches paper") (250 francs), and 750 copies on handmade paper (150 francs),[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-bbc/m001bvp2-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-105) plus an extra 20 unnumbered copies on mixed paper for libraries and press.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-The_National_Library_of_Ireland-108)
*   London: [Egoist Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Egoist_(periodical) "The Egoist (periodical)"), 1922: The first English edition published by [Harriet Shaw Weaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Shaw_Weaver "Harriet Shaw Weaver")'s Egoist Press in October 1922. For [legal reasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#Censorship) the book was printed on behalf of Egoist Press by [John Rodker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rodker "John Rodker") using the same printer, [Darantiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Darantiere?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maurice Darantiere (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice%20Darantiere "fr:Maurice Darantiere")], and plates as the first edition. This edition consisted of 2,000 numbered copies on handmade paper for sale[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-109) plus 100 unnumbered copies for press, publicity and [legal deposit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_deposit#United_Kingdom "Legal deposit") libraries.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-111)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-The_National_Library_of_Ireland-108)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-112) A seven-page [errata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errata "Errata") list compiled by Joyce, Weaver and Rodker was loosely inserted and contained 201 corrections.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-113)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-114) The [U.S. Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Post_Office "U.S. Post Office") reportedly burned up to 500 copies,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-115) as noted in later Shakespeare and Company editions.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-116)
*   New York: Two Worlds Publishing Company, 1929: The first U.S. edition of the novel was pirated by [Samuel Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Roth "Samuel Roth") without Joyce's authorisation, and first published serially in Roth's _Two Worlds Monthly_, then later in a single volume in 1929. It was designed to closely mimic the 1927 Shakespeare and Company 9th printing but many errors and corruptions occurred during reproduction.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-117)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-JJC-61) Reportedly 2,000–3,000 copies were printed but the majority were seized and destroyed by the [New York Society for the Suppression of Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Society_for_the_Suppression_of_Vice "New York Society for the Suppression of Vice") after a raid on Roth's offices on 4 October 1929[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-118)
*   Hamburg: Odyssey Press, 1932: In two volumes. The title page of this edition states "The present edition may be regarded as the definitive standard edition, as it has been specially revised, at the author's request, by [Stuart Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Gilbert "Stuart Gilbert")." This edition still contained errors but by its fourth revised printing (April 1939) it was considered the most accurate offering of the text and subsequently used as the basis for many later editions of the novel.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-later-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-120)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-JJC-61)
*   New York: Random House, 1934: The first authorised U.S. edition,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-121) published after the decision in _[United States v. One Book Called Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United\_States\_v.\_One\_Book\_Called\_Ulysses "United States v. One Book Called Ulysses")_ finding that the book was not obscene.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-later-119) Random House's founder [Bennett Cerf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_Cerf "Bennett Cerf") chose to base this edition on a copy of the pirated Samuel Roth edition of 1929, which led it to reproduce many of that edition's errors.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-122)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-123)
*   London: Bodley Head, 1936: The first edition printed and published in England. Set from the second impression of Odyssey Press's edition and purportedly proofed by Joyce.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-124)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-later-119)
*   Bodley Head, 1960: Newly reset corrected edition based on the 1958 impression of the earlier Bodley Head edition.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-OUP22-125) The source for many later editions by other publishers.
*   Random House, 1961: Reset from the 1960 Bodley Head edition.
*   _Ulysses: A Critical and Synoptic Edition_. Garland, 1984: Edited by Hans Walter Gabler.
*   _Ulysses: A Reader's Edition_. Lilliput Press, 1997: Edited by Danis Rose.

### "Joyce Wars"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: \"Joyce Wars\"")]

Hans Walter Gabler's 1984 edition was the most sustained attempt to produce a corrected text,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] but it has received much criticism, most notably[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] from [John Kidd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kidd_(scholar) "John Kidd (scholar)"). Kidd's main theoretical criticism is of Gabler's choice of a patchwork of manuscripts as his [copy-text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textual_criticism#Copy-text_editing "Textual criticism") (the base edition with which the editor compares each variant).[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-Kidd-126)

In June 1988, Kidd published "The Scandal of _Ulysses_" in _[The New York Review of Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Review\_of\_Books "The New York Review of Books")_,[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-Kidd-126) charging that not only did Gabler's changes overturn Joyce's last revisions, but in another 400 places Gabler failed to follow any manuscript whatever, making nonsense of his own premises. Kidd accused Gabler of unnecessarily changing Joyce's spelling, punctuation, use of accents, and all the details he claimed to have been restoring. Instead, Gabler was actually following printed editions such as that of 1932, not the manuscripts. Gabler was found to have made genuine blunders, such as his changing the name of the real-life Dubliner Harry Thrift to "Shrift" and cricketer Captain Buller to "Culler" on the basis of handwriting irregularities in the extant manuscript. (Gabler undid these "corrections" in 1986.) Kidd said that many of Gabler's errors resulted from his use of facsimiles rather than original manuscripts.

In December 1988, in "The New _Ulysses:_ The Hidden Controversy", Charles Rossman revealed that some of Gabler's own advisers felt that too many changes were being made, but that the publishers were pushing for as many alterations as possible. Then Kidd produced a 174-page critique that filled an entire issue of the _[Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papers\_of\_the\_Bibliographical\_Society\_of\_America "Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America")_, dated the same month.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-127) Kidd's James Joyce Research Center at [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") published this "Inquiry into _Ulysses_: The Corrected Text" the next year in book format and on [floppy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk").

Gabler and others, including Michael Groden, have rejected Kidd's critique. In his 1993 afterword to the Gabler edition, Groden writes that Kidd's lists of supposed errors were constructed "with so little demonstrated understanding of Gabler's theoretical assumptions and procedures... that they can point to errors or misjudgments only by accident". The scholarly community remains divided.

### Gabler edition replaced

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Gabler edition replaced")]

In 1990, Gabler's US publisher, Random House, after consulting a committee of scholars,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-128) replaced the Gabler edition with its 1961 version, and in the United Kingdom the Bodley Head press revived its 1960 version (upon which Random House's 1961 version is based). In both the UK and US, [Everyman's Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman's_Library "Everyman's Library") also republished the 1960 _Ulysses_. In 1992, [Penguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Books "Penguin Books") dropped Gabler and reprinted the 1960 text. The Gabler version remained available from Vintage International. Reprints of the 1922 first edition have also become widely available since 2012, when it entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") under [US copyright law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._copyright_law "U.S. copyright law").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-129)
